idiom_name: interface Events {} + addEventListener overloads and an unsubscribe closure
implementation_notes: TypeScript runs the same machinery as JavaScript - EventTarget in the DOM and in Node, EventEmitter on Node - and adds a compile-time contract: an interface mapping event names to payload types plus typed addEventListener/dispatchEvent overloads (or the generic EventEmitter<T> from the Node typings) makes the subscriber signature the compiler's business. It replaces the Observer interface with a typed listener map, so a wrong handler signature or a misspelled event name fails to compile. Keep an unsubscribe closure next to the subscription, because removeEventListener needs the identical function reference.
pitfalls: Typed listeners must be cast to EventListener for add/removeEventListener, so returning an unsubscribe closure (as above) is the only reliable removal path; otherwise you must keep the exact reference.
The event map only guards code that uses it: a plain string passed to dispatchEvent/emit compiles fine and fails at runtime.
Same leak semantics as JavaScript - a subscription strongly retains the listener and its captured state until the unsubscribe closure runs.
dispatchEvent is synchronous: a throwing listener surfaces as an uncaught error, and a listener that dispatches the same event recurses.

variants.name: RxJS Subject/Observable (functional streams)
variants.idiom_name: new Subject<T>() + pipe(...).subscribe(...) returning a Subscription
variants.implementation_notes: RxJS is the dominant functional realization in TypeScript codebases: new Subject<T>() (or BehaviorSubject for replay) is the publisher, subscribe(next) returns a Subscription with unsubscribe(), and Observable is the observer contract (next/error/complete) that operators such as filter, throttleTime and observeOn compose around. It replaces the listener registry and the update method with a stream, which pays off exactly when notifications need filtering, mapping, retries or scheduling; for one or two local callbacks the platform EventTarget is smaller and has no dependency.
pitfalls: Every subscribe must be unsubscribed, or terminated with takeUntil/takeWhile: leaked subscriptions keep firing and keep their observers alive.
A Subject is hot and multicast without replay - a subscriber that attaches late misses earlier values (BehaviorSubject/ReplaySubject change that contract).
An error notification completes the stream for all subscribers, so per-subscriber error handling belongs inside the pipe (catchError), not around subscribe.
Delivery is synchronous by default, so the emitting stack runs the whole operator chain; schedulers (observeOn/asyncScheduler) are a deliberate choice, not a default.
